name: Napoleonic Wars
summary: France under Napoleon fought most of Europe for twelve years and briefly dominated the continent.
body:
Part of [French Revolution](event:french-revolution). Nelson's victory at [Trafalgar](event:trafalgar) secured British command of the sea; the [invasion of Russia](event:russia-1812) destroyed the Grande Armée; [Waterloo](event:waterloo) ended the adventure.

The wars spread the Napoleonic Code, conscription and nationalism across Europe, and the peace that followed at Vienna held the great powers back from general war for a century — until [1914](event:ww1).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleonic_Wars).

name: Battle of Trafalgar
summary: Nelson destroyed the combined French and Spanish fleets off Cadiz, ending any prospect of invading Britain.
body:
Part of [Napoleonic Wars](event:napoleonic-wars). Nelson destroyed the combined French and Spanish fleets off Cadiz, ending any prospect of invading Britain.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Trafalgar).

name: Battle of Austerlitz
summary: A feigned weakness drew the Austro-Russian army onto ground of Napoleon's choosing.
body:
Part of [Napoleonic Wars](event:napoleonic-wars). Napoleon feigned weakness to draw the Austro-Russian army onto ground of his choosing, and the resulting battle was a decisive French victory.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Austerlitz).

name: Latin American wars of independence
summary: Spain and Portugal lost almost all of their American empires within a generation.
body:
Bolívar and San Martín campaigned from Venezuela to Peru; Brazil separated from Portugal without a general war. The new republics inherited enormous inequality and unstable borders.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_American_wars_of_independence).

name: French invasion of Russia
summary: An army of some 600,000 marched to Moscow; fewer than a tenth came back.
body:
Part of [Napoleonic Wars](event:napoleonic-wars). An army of some 600,000 marched to Moscow; fewer than a tenth came back.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_invasion_of_Russia).

name: Battle of Waterloo
summary: Wellington held the ridge until the Prussians arrived; Napoleon abdicated four days later and died in exile on St Helena.
body:
Part of [Napoleonic Wars](event:napoleonic-wars). Wellington held the ridge until the Prussians arrived; Napoleon abdicated four days later and died in exile on St Helena.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Waterloo).

name: Eruption of Tambora
summary: The largest eruption in recorded history threw enough sulphate into the stratosphere to cool the whole planet.
body:
Tens of thousands died on Sumbawa; far more died in the [famines of the following year](event:year-without-summer).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1815_eruption_of_Mount_Tambora).

name: The Year Without a Summer
summary: Snow fell in New England in June and harvests failed across Europe and Asia, causing the worst famine of the century.
body:
Part of [Eruption of Tambora](event:tambora). Kept indoors by the weather at Lake Geneva, Mary Shelley wrote *Frankenstein*.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_Without_a_Summer).

name: First passenger railway
summary: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened, the first intercity line worked entirely by steam locomotives.
body:
Part of [Industrial Revolution](event:industrial-revolution). Within thirty years rail networks covered Britain, Europe and the eastern United States, sharply reducing travel times and prompting the adoption of standard time.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_and_Manchester_Railway).

name: Opium Wars
summary: Britain forced China to keep importing opium, taking Hong Kong and a series of unequal treaties.
body:
The wars began the period of foreign dominance known in Chinese historiography as the "century of humiliation", which ended imperial China and has shaped Chinese foreign policy to this day.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opium_Wars).

name: Electric telegraph
summary: Morse's Washington–Baltimore line separated communication from transport for the first time in history.
body:
By 1866 a working cable crossed the Atlantic, cutting the time for a message from London to New York from ten days to minutes.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_telegraph).

name: First public demonstration of ether anesthesia
summary: William Morton demonstrated that ether vapour could render a patient painless during surgery at Massachusetts General Hospital.
body:
Surgery before the 1840s was carried out without effective pain relief. Morton's demonstration on October 16, 1846 showed that ether could render a patient insensible, though chloroform soon became the preferred agent in Europe.

The ability to operate without pain opened surgery to procedures that had been unthinkable, and together with [germ theory](event:germ-theory) it began to make the operating theatre survivable.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_general_anesthesia).

name: Revolutions of 1848
summary: Liberal and nationalist uprisings swept some fifty European states within months; nearly all were suppressed within two years.
body:
Liberal and nationalist uprisings swept some fifty European states within months; nearly all were suppressed within two years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutions_of_1848).

name: The Communist Manifesto
summary: Marx and Engels published a short pamphlet arguing that history is driven by class struggle.
body:
It became the founding text of a movement that would govern a third of humanity in the twentieth century — see the [Russian Revolution](event:russian-revolution) and [the founding of the PRC](event:prc-founded).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Communist_Manifesto).

name: Taiping Rebellion
summary: A millenarian movement led by a man who believed he was Jesus's younger brother held southern China for a decade; 20–30 million died.
body:
It is among the deadliest wars in history, and it broke the finances and the prestige of the [Qing](event:qing-dynasty).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiping_Rebellion).

name: Crimean War
summary: Britain, France and the Ottoman Empire fought Russia over influence in the Black Sea and the Holy Land, and over the fate of a declining Ottoman Empire.
body:
The war saw the first modern war correspondents and photographers, and brought Florence Nightingale's reform of military nursing. It also introduced the rifle-musket and trench warfare that would reappear, far deadlier, in [1914](event:ww1).

The Russian defeat checked tsarist expansion for a generation, and the Treaty of Paris neutralised the Black Sea — terms Russia repudiated as soon as the other powers were distracted in 1870. Defeat also pushed St Petersburg into the reforms that ended serfdom.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimean_War).

name: Bessemer steel process
summary: Henry Bessemer's process converted pig iron to steel in bulk, cutting costs and making railroads and armaments much cheaper.
body:
Part of [Industrial Revolution](event:industrial-revolution). The Bessemer converter used a blast of air to burn away carbon impurities, a method simple and cheap enough that within a generation steel had replaced iron for most purposes.

The result was [railways](event:railways) that covered continents and ships that were faster and more durable, along with the steel navies and artillery that the powers built in the decades before [World War I](event:ww1).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessemer_process).

name: Indian Rebellion
summary: Indian soldiers and civilians rose against the East India Company, nearly expelling the British from the subcontinent before being brutally suppressed.
body:
Part of the [East India Company](event:english-east-india) era in India. The rebellion — sparked partly by rumours that new cartridges were greased with animal fat offensive to Hindu and Muslim soldiers — spread across the north, lasted over a year, and cost hundreds of thousands of lives, most of them Indian.

Its suppression was ferocious, with mass reprisals against civilians. The Crown took direct control from the Company and brought India more firmly into the Empire, but the uprising had shown that British rule was neither inevitable nor unopposed — a lesson that would echo through the next ninety years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Rebellion_of_1857).

name: First transatlantic telegraph cable
summary: A submarine telegraph cable successfully crossed the Atlantic, connecting North America to Europe and shortening communication from ten days to minutes.
body:
Part of [Electric telegraph](event:telegraph). After three failed attempts, the cable laid in 1858 worked for three weeks before failing — but that was enough to show the feasibility. The cable of 1866 endured and opened a new era of real-time global communication.

It made possible the instantaneous coordination of ship movements, stock prices and news across an ocean, binding the Atlantic economy into one system.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transatlantic_telegraph_cable).

name: British Raj
summary: The Crown took over direct rule of India from the East India Company after the rebellion of 1857.
body:
Railways, telegraphs and English-language institutions coexisted with deindustrialisation and repeated devastating famines. It ended with [independence and partition](event:indian-independence).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Raj).

name: Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species
summary: Natural selection explained the diversity and design of life without a designer.
body:
Darwin had sat on the idea for twenty years; Alfred Russel Wallace's independent arrival at the same conclusion forced publication. The theory unified all of biology and, with [genetics](event:dna-structure), remains its central organising principle.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Origin_of_Species).

name: Germ theory of disease
summary: Pasteur, Koch and Lister established that specific microorganisms cause specific diseases.
body:
Antisepsis, pasteurisation, sterile surgery and public sanitation followed; combined with later [antibiotics](event:penicillin) and [vaccination](event:smallpox-vaccine), they roughly doubled human life expectancy.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germ_theory_of_disease).

name: American Civil War
summary: The United States fought its bloodiest war over slavery and secession; some 700,000 died.
body:
The [Emancipation Proclamation](event:emancipation) turned the war into a war against [slavery](event:slave-trade); [Gettysburg](event:gettysburg) broke the Confederate offensive; [Lincoln was assassinated](event:lincoln-assassination) days after the surrender at Appomattox.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War).

name: Emancipation Proclamation
summary: Lincoln declared enslaved people in the rebelling states to be free; the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery outright in 1865.
body:
Part of [American Civil War](event:us-civil-war). Lincoln declared enslaved people in the rebelling states to be free; the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery outright in 1865.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emancipation_Proclamation).

name: Battle of Gettysburg
summary: Three days of fighting in Pennsylvania ended Lee's invasion of the North.
body:
Part of [American Civil War](event:us-civil-war). Three days of fighting in Pennsylvania ended Lee's invasion of the North.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Gettysburg).

name: Assassination of Abraham Lincoln
summary: Lincoln was shot at Ford's Theatre five days after Lee's surrender.
body:
Part of [American Civil War](event:us-civil-war). Lincoln was shot at Ford's Theatre five days after Lee's surrender.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Abraham_Lincoln).

name: Meiji Restoration
summary: Japan abolished the shogunate and deliberately industrialised, becoming a great power within a generation.
body:
Within forty years of [ending its isolation](event:edo-japan) Japan had defeated Russia at sea — the first modern victory of an Asian state over a European empire.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meiji_Restoration).

name: Suez Canal opens
summary: A sea-level canal between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea cut thousands of kilometres from the Europe–Asia route.
body:
A sea-level canal between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea cut thousands of kilometres from the Europe–Asia route.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suez_Canal).

name: First transcontinental railroad
summary: The golden spike at Promontory Summit joined the American rail network coast to coast.
body:
Part of [First passenger railway](event:railways). The golden spike at Promontory Summit joined the American rail network coast to coast.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_transcontinental_railroad).

name: Mendeleev's periodic table
summary: Arranging the elements by weight and property revealed a periodic law — and gaps where undiscovered elements had to be.
body:
Arranging the elements by weight and property revealed a periodic law — and gaps where undiscovered elements had to be.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_table).

name: Metre Convention standardises metric system
summary: Seventeen nations agreed on standard definitions of the metre and kilogram, making the metric system international.
body:
France had built the metric system during the [Revolution](event:french-revolution), but for decades it spread slowly and Britain in particular resisted it. The 1875 Convention created shared prototypes of the metre and kilogram and the Bureau International des Poids et Mesures outside Paris to keep them.

Its successor, the SI, is now the legal basis of measurement in almost every country, and the treaty bodies founded in 1875 still define the units that science and trade depend on.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metre_Convention).

name: Telephone
summary: Alexander Graham Bell patented a device that carried the human voice over a wire.
body:
Alexander Graham Bell patented a device that carried the human voice over a wire.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telephone).

name: Edison's phonograph
summary: Thomas Edison built the first device that could both record sound and play it back, capturing a voice on a cylinder wrapped in tinfoil.
body:
Early phonographs were crude; Edison's first recording was "Mary Had a Little Lamb". Within a decade the device was manufactured commercially. By the early twentieth century the gramophone and flat disc records were displacing it, but Edison had shown that sound could be captured, stored and retrieved.

Recording separated music from live performance, and a performance could now outlast the performer. A commercial recording industry followed, and the problem of reproducing sound faithfully later shaped broadcasting and [sound film](event:jazz-singer).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phonograph).

name: Practical electric lighting
summary: Edison's long-lasting incandescent lamp, and the generating stations built to supply it, electrified cities.
body:
Edison's long-lasting incandescent lamp, and the generating stations built to supply it, electrified cities.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incandescent_light_bulb).

name: Modern global warming
summary: Greenhouse gases released since the Industrial Revolution have warmed the planet by about 1.3 °C, and the rate is increasing.
body:
Atmospheric CO2 has risen from about 280 ppm before the [Industrial Revolution](event:industrial-revolution) to over 420 ppm. Ice sheets and glaciers are losing mass, sea level is rising, and extreme heat has become measurably more frequent.

The [Montreal Protocol](event:montreal-protocol) and the [Paris Agreement](event:paris-agreement) are the main treaty responses; the geological analogue is the [PETM](event:petm), 56 million years ago.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_warming).

name: Scramble for Africa
summary: European powers partitioned almost the entire African continent among themselves in three decades.
body:
The Berlin Conference of 1884–85 set the rules; the borders drawn then are largely those of Africa today. Conquest was brutal — the Congo Free State alone may have cost millions of lives — and was undone only by [decolonisation](event:decolonisation) after 1945.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scramble_for_Africa).

name: Eruption of Krakatoa
summary: The explosion was heard 4,800 km away and the tsunamis it raised killed more than 36,000 people.
body:
It was the first global disaster reported worldwide within hours, by [telegraph](event:telegraph).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1883_eruption_of_Krakatoa).

name: Kodak roll film camera
summary: George Eastman produced the first camera using roll film and affordable for amateurs, putting photography in ordinary hands.
body:
Photography before 1888 required glass plates, darkrooms and chemical expertise. The Kodak camera with roll film cost $25 and worked simply: the user exposed the frame, returned the camera to the factory, and received prints and a reloaded camera.

This put photography within reach of the general public. By 1900 millions of amateur photographs existed; by 1945 personal photography was routine, and the documentary power of the image was transforming warfare and politics.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kodak).

name: Guglielmo Marconi and wireless telegraphy
summary: Marconi transmitted radio signals without wires, solving the problem of communication to moving ships and remote locations.
body:
Building on the discoveries of Hertz and others, Marconi was the first to make wireless transmission practical. By 1897 he was operating a station on the Isle of Wight; in 1901 he claimed the first signal across the Atlantic.

Wireless proved its worth at sea: the distress calls sent from the [Titanic](event:titanic-sinks) in 1912 brought the Carpathia to the lifeboats, and the disaster led to international rules requiring a continuous radio watch. By the 1920s the same technology had become a mass broadcast medium.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guglielmo_Marconi).

name: Discovery of X-rays
summary: Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays while experimenting with cathode tubes, opening a new window into the human body and atom.
body:
On November 8, 1895, Röntgen found that a cathode tube emitted an invisible radiation that passed through flesh but was absorbed by bone, producing the first image of a living skeleton made without dissection.

X-rays allowed diagnosis without cutting, and became a tool for probing the structure of matter, from crystals to the atom itself. The discovery also set others hunting for similar rays, and [radioactivity](event:radioactivity) was found the following year.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray).

name: Cuban War of Independence
summary: Cuban insurgents fought Spanish rule for three years before American intervention in 1898 ended Spain's empire in the Americas and left the United States dominant on the island.
body:
The Cuban rising had been running for three years when the United States intervened in 1898. The Spanish-American War that followed lasted about ten weeks.

Spain lost its last major colony. Cuba became nominally independent but remained under American occupation, with American companies dominant in the sugar economy. The war marked the emergence of the United States as a global power and began half a century of American military intervention in Latin America.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_War_of_Independence).

name: Discovery of radioactivity
summary: Henri Becquerel found that uranium salts emit radiation of their own accord, and Marie and Pierre Curie went on to isolate new radioactive elements.
body:
Becquerel observed that uranium salts emitted radiation without being heated or exposed to light, indicating that the energy came from inside the atom. The Curies followed in 1898 by isolating polonium and radium, showing that some atoms are simply unstable.

Radioactivity opened the study of atomic structure. It provided a new energy source, allowed the dating of rocks and fossils, and showed that the transmutation of elements was real. It led to [nuclear fission](event:nuclear-fission) and the [atomic bomb](event:trinity).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive_decay).

name: Boxer Rebellion
summary: Chinese militia rose against foreign influence and Christian missionaries, besieging foreign legations in Beijing and prompting an international military response.
body:
The Boxers sought to expel foreigners and restore Qing authority. They failed, but the uprising exposed the fault lines between Chinese nationalism and European imperialism.

An eight-nation relief force, to which Japan contributed the largest contingent, broke the siege of the legations in August 1900; the occupying troops then looted Beijing. The indemnity imposed on China crippled its finances for a generation and pushed the country toward revolution. The campaign also showed that the European powers could act together against a non-European state, a lesson noted in Japan.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxer_Rebellion).

name: Second Boer War
summary: British and colonial forces subdued the Afrikaner republics of South Africa, absorbing them into the Empire and sowing decades of resentment.
body:
The war began with a Boer invasion but turned into a counterinsurgency in which British forces burned farms and moved civilians into internment camps, the first widespread use of the term concentration camp. Disease and shortages killed roughly 28,000 Boer internees, most of them children, and at least 20,000 Black African internees.

The war showed that European military superiority was no longer automatic, cost Britain £200 million, an immense sum for the time, and was bitterly divisive at home. The peace preserved Boer identity and property, but the scorched-earth tactics and racial hierarchy shaped South Africa for a century.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Boer_War).

name: First powered flight
summary: The Wright brothers flew a heavier-than-air powered machine under control at Kitty Hawk.
body:
Sixty-six years separate that 12-second hop from the [Moon landing](event:moon-landing).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wright_Flyer).

name: Suffragette movement in Britain
summary: British women, denied the vote, escalated from petitions to property damage and hunger strikes, forcing the question of female enfranchisement onto the political agenda.
body:
Emmeline Pankhurst and her daughters adopted militant tactics — arson, bombing, slashing paintings — that terrified the establishment and fascinated the press. The campaign was suspended during [World War I](event:ww1) but resumed after, resulting in limited suffrage in 1918 and full suffrage in 1928.

The movement divided campaigners themselves: constitutional suffragists, far more numerous, argued that militancy set the cause back. But their visibility made the cause impossible to ignore, and their sacrifice — prison, force-feeding — gave moral weight to the claim that democracy without women was a sham.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffragette).

name: Russo-Japanese War
summary: Japan and Russia fought for control of Korea and Manchuria; Japan's victory proved that an Asian power could defeat a European empire.
body:
Japan's navy destroyed two Russian fleets, and its army outmanoeuvred Russian conscripts on land. The Treaty of Portsmouth (1905) required Russia to cede territory and influence, and the defeat helped touch off the revolution of 1905 that shook the tsarist state a decade before [1917](event:russian-revolution).

The victory showed that an Asian power could defeat a European empire in the field, and it changed perceptions of European military dominance from Turkey to China to India. Japan itself, emboldened, continued its expansion toward [empire](event:meiji).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Japanese_War).

name: Einstein's theory of relativity
summary: Einstein's relativity described space and time as aspects of a single flexible geometry, and mass as a form of energy.
body:
Special relativity (1905) resolved the incompatibility between mechanics and electromagnetism. General relativity (1915) recast gravity as the curvature of spacetime, and was confirmed in 1919 by observations of starlight bending around the sun.

GPS, black holes, cosmology and [gravitational waves](event:gravitational-waves) all follow from it.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theory_of_relativity).

name: Finland grants women's suffrage
summary: Finland became the first European nation to grant women full voting and candidacy rights.
body:
Women had already voted elsewhere, in the Wyoming Territory from 1869 and New Zealand from 1893, but Finland was the first country to give women both the vote and the right to stand for election.

The reform was tied to Finland's struggle for independence from Russia, and women's part in the national movement strengthened their claim. The new single-chamber parliament created in 1906 was elected on universal suffrage, and nineteen women took seats in it the following year. Other Nordic countries followed within decades, then Britain and the United States, though many nations did not enfranchise women until after [World War II](event:ww2).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women%27s_suffrage_in_Finland).

name: Bosnian Crisis
summary: Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia-Herzegovina, triggering a crisis with Russia and Serbia that brought Europe close to war six years before [1914](event:ww1).
body:
The crisis revealed the brittleness of the European order. Austria's move violated the Treaty of Berlin; Serbia wanted Bosnia for itself; Russia claimed to defend Slavic interests; Germany backed Austria. For a moment the powers seemed on the brink of war.

Russia backed down, but the humiliation fuelled Slavic nationalism and Russian desire for revenge. The Balkans had become the flashpoint where ethnic, great-power and religious interests collided — a role it would maintain through [1945](event:ww2) and beyond.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosnian_crisis_of_1908%E2%80%9309).

name: Blériot's Channel crossing
summary: Louis Blériot flew a monoplane across the English Channel, proving that aircraft could make practical journeys and making invasion by air conceivable.
body:
The [Wright brothers](event:wright-flyer) had flown, but Blériot's 1909 crossing showed that an aircraft could be taken where the aviator chose. The flight took 36 minutes, and the sea that had protected Britain for a thousand years was no longer an obstacle.

The implications were military. Within a few years aircraft were being armed, and by [1914](event:ww1) they were flying reconnaissance over the front.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Blériot).

name: Scott's Antarctic Expedition
summary: Robert Falcon Scott led an expedition to the South Pole, reaching it only to find he had been beaten by Amundsen; he and his party died on the return.
body:
Scott's journey to the South Pole in 1911-1912 was a race against Roald Amundsen, who used sled dogs and reached the Pole on 14 December 1911, five weeks ahead of him. Scott's party man-hauled its sledges in temperatures below -40 °C, and the method proved fatal. He died about eleven miles from One Ton Depot.

His final letters were found with his body and made him a national figure in Britain. The expedition combined scientific work in meteorology, geology and biology with the imperial prestige of exploration, a late episode of the [Age of Discovery](event:age-of-discovery) before the world was fully mapped.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terra_Nova_Expedition).

name: Xinhai Revolution ends the Qing dynasty
summary: The Xinhai Revolution ended more than two and a half centuries of Qing rule and over two thousand years of imperial government, installing a republic that soon fractured under warlords.
body:
The Qing dynasty fell suddenly, after an accidental bomb explosion, a failed cover-up and military mutinies in a dozen cities. The last emperor, a child, abdicated in February 1912. Sun Yat-sen's republic took its place but lacked the power to govern.

Fifteen years of warlord division followed, then [Japanese invasion](event:sino-japanese-war) and civil war between Nationalists and Communists. The revolution ended the assumption that China would be ruled by dynasties, and later Chinese conflicts turned on ideology rather than imperial succession.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinhai_Revolution).

name: RMS Titanic sinks
summary: The "unsinkable" liner struck an iceberg and sank in the North Atlantic, killing about 1,500 people.
body:
Titanic was the largest ship afloat and reflected the period's confidence in engineering. It struck an iceberg at night and sank in under three hours, killing about 1,500 people. There were lifeboats for barely half those aboard, and survival rates fell sharply with class: most women in first class survived, while the majority of third-class passengers did not.

The disaster prompted new rules requiring lifeboat capacity for everyone aboard and a continuous wireless watch at sea, and it undercut the Edwardian assumption that technology had made travel fundamentally safe.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanic).

name: Ford assembly line
summary: Henry Ford introduced the moving assembly line to automobile manufacturing, allowing mass production and making cars affordable for ordinary workers.
body:
The assembly line cut the time to assemble a Model T from 12 hours to 93 minutes. By the early 1920s the Model T accounted for roughly half the cars on earth, and a worker on Ford's five-dollar day could afford one.

Cheap cars made suburbs possible and commuting normal. Ford's mass production methods were copied worldwide, from Soviet tractor plants to Japanese electronics manufacturing.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assembly_line).

name: Panama Canal opens
summary: A canal of locks and an artificial lake joined the Atlantic and Pacific, cutting some 13,000 kilometres from the voyage between New York and San Francisco.
body:
The French had attempted a sea-level cut and failed. The Americans succeeded with locks, a dammed lake and a mosquito-control campaign that finally curbed yellow fever, though malaria and accidents still killed thousands of workers. The first ship transited on August 15, 1914, weeks after [World War I](event:ww1) began in Europe.

The canal let the United States move a fleet between the Atlantic and the Pacific and strengthened its position in the Caribbean. Washington governed the surrounding Canal Zone as its own territory until 1979 and kept control of the waterway until 1999.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama_Canal).

name: World War I
summary: Four years of industrial-scale war killed some 20 million people and destroyed four empires.
body:
An [assassination in Sarajevo](event:sarajevo) triggered interlocking alliances; machine guns and artillery made the [Western Front](event:somme) a stalemate of trenches for four years. Russia collapsed into [revolution](event:russian-revolution); the United States entered in 1917.

The [Treaty of Versailles](event:versailles) redrew Europe and the Middle East, and left grievances that contributed directly to [the next war](event:ww2).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I).

name: Assassination of Franz Ferdinand
summary: Gavrilo Princip shot the Austrian heir in Sarajevo, setting off the July Crisis.
body:
Part of [World War I](event:ww1). Gavrilo Princip shot the Austrian heir in Sarajevo, setting off the July Crisis.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Archduke_Franz_Ferdinand).

name: Easter Rising in Dublin
summary: Irish republicans seized buildings in central Dublin and proclaimed a republic; the rising was crushed within a week, but its aftermath reshaped Irish politics.
body:
The rebellion was crushed in a week, and sixteen rebel leaders were executed by firing squad. But their deaths transformed them into martyrs — Irish public opinion, previously divided on independence, swung decisively against British rule.

Sinn Féin swept the 1918 election on that changed mood, and the war that followed produced [the Irish Free State](event:irish-independence) in 1921.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easter_Rising).

name: Battle of Verdun
summary: Ten months of attrition around a French fortress city cost some 700,000 casualties.
body:
Part of [World War I](event:ww1). Ten months of attrition around a French fortress city cost some 700,000 casualties.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Verdun).

name: Battle of the Somme
summary: Nearly 60,000 British casualties fell on the first day; tanks appeared in battle for the first time.
body:
Part of [World War I](event:ww1). Nearly 60,000 British casualties fell on the first day; tanks appeared in battle for the first time.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Somme).

name: Russian Revolution
summary: Tsarism fell and the Bolsheviks built the world's first communist state.
body:
The February revolution ended the monarchy; the [October revolution](event:october-revolution) put Lenin in power; a civil war of five years followed, and the [Soviet Union](event:ussr-founded) was formed in 1922.

It made [communism](event:communist-manifesto) a governing ideology and set up the [Cold War](event:cold-war) that dominated the century's second half.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Revolution).

name: October Revolution
summary: Bolshevik forces seized the Winter Palace and the organs of the Provisional Government in Petrograd.
body:
Part of [Russian Revolution](event:russian-revolution). Bolshevik forces seized the Winter Palace and the organs of the Provisional Government in Petrograd.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_Revolution).

name: Spanish flu pandemic
summary: An H1N1 influenza pandemic infected perhaps a third of humanity and killed 50 million or more.
body:
It spread along the troop movements of [the First World War](event:ww1), and unusually killed healthy young adults. Wartime censorship kept it out of the news everywhere except neutral Spain — hence the misleading name.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_flu).

name: Treaty of Versailles
summary: The peace imposed on Germany assigned it war guilt and reparations, and redrew the map of Europe.
body:
Part of [World War I](event:ww1). The peace imposed on Germany assigned it war guilt and reparations, and redrew the map of Europe.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Versailles).

name: American Prohibition
summary: The United States banned the manufacture, sale and transport of alcohol, creating a massive black market and empowering organized crime.
body:
Prohibition was intended as a moral and public health reform, backed by progressive reformers and churches. In practice it criminalised millions of ordinary citizens and created large illegal markets; Al Capone's Chicago bootleg empire was built on it.

The policy showed the limits of law that lacks popular support. By 1933 even conservative politicians accepted that Prohibition had failed, and the Twenty-first Amendment repealed the Eighteenth, the first and only repeal of an amendment to the United States Constitution.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prohibition_in_the_United_States).

name: Irish independence
summary: After a two-year war of independence, the Anglo-Irish Treaty created the Irish Free State as a dominion and partitioned the island.
body:
The war lasted 1919-1921 and was brutal — British auxiliary police burned Irish towns, Irish rebels killed suspected informers. The settlement partitioned the island, with six northern counties remaining in the United Kingdom.

The Free State was a compromise that satisfied neither republican purists nor Ulster unionists. But it established the principle that the British Empire's grip on its territories was not absolute — a lesson that would reshape the [decolonisation](event:decolonisation) of the twentieth century.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_War_of_Independence).

name: Discovery of insulin
summary: Frederick Banting and Charles Best extracted insulin from the pancreas, providing the first effective treatment for diabetes and saving millions of lives.
body:
Before insulin, type 1 diabetes was fatal, causing a slow decline through hyperglycemia and ketoacidosis. Banting's team found that pancreatic extracts lowered blood sugar, and within a year insulin was being mass-produced and injected into diabetics.

The first patient, a fourteen-year-old boy, went from near-death to recovery, and millions who would have died could now be treated. The finding that the pancreas regulates blood sugar also opened the field of endocrinology.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insulin).

name: Soviet Union founded
summary: The union treaty created the USSR, which would last until [1991](event:soviet-collapse).
body:
Part of [Russian Revolution](event:russian-revolution). The union treaty created the USSR, which would last until [1991](event:soviet-collapse).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union).

name: Great Kanto earthquake
summary: A magnitude 7.9 earthquake destroyed Tokyo and Yokohama, killing over 100,000 people and shaking faith in urban progress.
body:
The earthquake struck at midday, when most cooking stoves were lit, and fires spread unchecked through Tokyo and Yokohama. Most of the dead were killed by the firestorms rather than by the shaking itself; a single fire whirl in Tokyo's Honjo district killed tens of thousands sheltering in an open yard.

Reconstruction was rapid, and Tokyo was rebuilt on a larger scale. In the chaos, false rumours that Koreans were poisoning wells and setting fires led to massacres by vigilante groups in which thousands of Korean residents were killed, and the rebuilding strained Japanese public finances for years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1923_Great_Kant%C5%8D_earthquake).

name: Scopes Monkey Trial
summary: A Tennessee schoolteacher was prosecuted for teaching evolution, putting [Darwin's theory](event:origin-species) on trial before a national radio audience.
body:
John Scopes was fined $100 for violating a state law against teaching that humans descended from animals. William Jennings Bryan prosecuted and Clarence Darrow defended, and the proceedings were broadcast live on radio, the first trial to reach an audience of millions.

Scopes was convicted, though the verdict was overturned on a technicality. The case exposed a division in American culture between scientific consensus on [Darwin's theory](event:origin-species) and religious conviction, a division that persisted long after the trial.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scopes_trial).

name: British General Strike
summary: British coal miners struck over wage cuts, joined by millions of other workers in the only general strike in British history.
body:
For nine days in May 1926, Britain was partially paralysed: trains, buses and newspapers stopped. The government and middle-class volunteers kept essential services running. The strike coalition fractured, and miners returned to worse terms than they had refused before the stoppage.

The strike exposed the weakness of Britain's economic position after [World War I](event:ww1) and the depth of its class divisions. It also convinced much of the union movement that its future lay in parliamentary politics through the Labour Party rather than in mass industrial action.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1926_United_Kingdom_general_strike).

name: Lindbergh's transatlantic flight
summary: Charles Lindbergh flew the Spirit of St. Louis from New York to Paris in 33 hours, proving that aircraft could cross an ocean safely and thrilling the world.
body:
Lindbergh was twenty-five, relatively unknown, and flying alone. When he landed at Le Bourget airfield after 33 hours, a crowd of more than a hundred thousand surged onto the field, and newspapers sold millions of copies carrying his photograph.

The flight showed that aviation was not confined to exhibition and military use. Where [wireless](event:wireless-telegraphy) had freed messages from ships, aircraft now began to free travellers from them: airmail contracts and airline investment followed, and scheduled transatlantic services began within little more than a decade.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Lindbergh).

name: The Jazz Singer — first sound film
summary: The first commercially successful motion picture with synchronized sound transformed cinema overnight from pantomime to dialogue.
body:
Silent film had been an international form: a German film could be shown anywhere. Sound tied film to language, and American control of the technology meant English-language cinema came to dominate world markets.

Actors with good voices became valuable, while those with poor diction lost work. Converting theatres to sound was expensive. Silent production ended within five years, the established silent comedians struggled to adapt, and cinema became a medium of dialogue as much as gesture.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Jazz_Singer).

name: Invention of television
summary: Philo Farnsworth transmitted the first all-electronic television image, the basis of the medium that would shape the second half of the twentieth century.
body:
Philo Farnsworth, a twenty-one-year-old from a farm in Idaho, transmitted the first electronic television image, a single horizontal line, on September 7, 1927. Vladimir Zworykin, then at Westinghouse and later at RCA, was developing rival camera and display tubes over the same years, and the competing claims led to a long patent fight that Farnsworth largely won.

Electronic television was far better than the mechanical alternatives, and by the late 1930s it was becoming commercial. [World War II](event:ww2) delayed mass adoption, but by 1950 television was becoming a presence in American homes, and it went on to reshape news, politics and entertainment.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_television).

name: Discovery of penicillin
summary: Alexander Fleming noticed that a stray mould killed bacteria on a forgotten culture plate.
body:
Mass production from 1943 gave medicine its first reliable cure for bacterial infection and saved many millions of lives.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penicillin).

name: Great Depression
summary: The deepest economic collapse of the industrial age: a quarter of American workers unemployed, world trade down by two thirds.
body:
It began with the [Wall Street crash](event:wall-street-crash), spread through the gold standard and banking failures, and produced both the New Deal and the political conditions for [fascism in Europe](event:ww2).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression).

name: Wall Street crash
summary: The New York stock market lost a third of its value in weeks, wiping out fortunes and confidence alike.
body:
Part of [Great Depression](event:great-depression). The New York stock market lost a third of its value in weeks, wiping out fortunes and confidence alike.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street_Crash_of_1929).

name: The Dust Bowl
summary: Drought and ploughed-up prairie grass turned the southern Great Plains into moving dunes, displacing hundreds of thousands.
body:
Part of [Great Depression](event:great-depression). Drought and ploughed-up prairie grass turned the southern Great Plains into moving dunes, displacing hundreds of thousands.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dust_Bowl).

name: Gandhi's Salt March
summary: Gandhi walked 385 km to the sea to make salt in defiance of the British monopoly, launching mass civil disobedience.
body:
Part of [British Raj](event:british-raj). His method of non-violent resistance directly influenced the [American civil rights movement](event:civil-rights).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_March).

name: Japanese invasion of Manchuria
summary: Japanese military forces seized Manchuria from China, the first major aggression by a revisionist power in the post-[World War I](event:ww1) era.
body:
The League of Nations condemned the invasion but took no action. Japan then withdrew from the League and began rearming openly. The Manchurian conquest set a pattern in which aggression met protest rather than force.

Japan's success encouraged similar moves by Mussolini in Abyssinia in 1935 and Hitler in the Rhineland in 1936. The democracies lacked the will to enforce the rules they had created, and the result was a slide toward [World War II](event:ww2).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invasion_of_Manchuria).

name: Hitler appointed Chancellor of Germany
summary: President Hindenburg appointed Adolf Hitler Chancellor, believing he could be controlled and that the appointment would end Germany's political paralysis.
body:
The Nazis had taken 37% of the vote in July 1932 and fallen back to 33% in November, making them the largest party in the Reichstag but far short of a majority. Conservatives around Hindenburg brokered the appointment in the belief that they could use and contain Hitler.

Within two months the Reichstag fire decree had suspended civil liberties and the [Enabling Act](event:enabling-act) had given him the power to legislate alone. Within six, opposition parties were banned, thousands of opponents were held in the first camps, and Germany was a one-party state.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machtergreifung).

name: Enabling Act in Nazi Germany
summary: The Reichstag voted to grant Hitler the power to make laws without parliament, effectively ending democracy in Germany and enabling the Holocaust.
body:
The vote was 444-94. The Social Democrats voted against; the Communist deputies had already been arrested or driven into hiding and could not vote at all. The Centre Party and the conservative right voted in favour, expecting that they could limit how the powers were used. Hitler used them to ban parties, purge the civil service and build the machinery of a totalitarian state.

The Enabling Act ended parliamentary government in Weimar Germany. Within a year the country had one party, one leader and no mechanism for peaceful change. [World War II](event:ww2) and the [Holocaust](event:holocaust) followed from this vote.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enabling_Act_of_1933).

name: Italian invasion of Abyssinia
summary: Mussolini's forces invaded Ethiopia, one of only two African states that had kept their independence, and used chemical weapons against its army and civilians.
body:
The League of Nations imposed sanctions, but they were incomplete and ineffective: oil, essential to Italy's war machine, was not embargoed. Italy used mustard gas against Ethiopian soldiers and civilians, the first large-scale use of chemical weapons since [World War I](event:ww1).

Italy's aggression went unopposed and showed that the League could not enforce its rules. Hitler took note and reoccupied the Rhineland the following year. The path to [World War II](event:ww2) was paved by such acts of revisionist aggression left unchecked.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Italo-Ethiopian_War).

name: Spanish Civil War
summary: Franco's nationalists, backed by Germany and Italy, defeated the Republic in a war that served as a rehearsal for [the world war](event:ww2).
body:
Franco's nationalists, backed by Germany and Italy, defeated the Republic. The conflict let the fascist powers test equipment and tactics, and [World War II](event:ww2) began a few months after it ended.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Civil_War).

name: Second Sino-Japanese War
summary: Japan launched a full-scale invasion of China, occupying much of the country in an eight-year war that killed millions and later merged into [World War II](event:ww2).
body:
The war began with an incident at Marco Polo Bridge and escalated to the occupation of Shanghai, Nanjing and most of coastal China. Japanese forces committed mass atrocities against civilians and prisoners; at Nanjing in 1937, estimates of those killed range from tens of thousands to 300,000.

The war lasted eight years and killed an estimated fifteen to twenty million Chinese, most of them civilians. It merged into [World War II](event:ww2) when Japan attacked the United States in 1941. Chinese resistance, nominally unified under Chiang Kai-shek but in fact fragmented between Nationalists and Communists, proved crucial to the eventual defeat of Japan.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Sino-Japanese_War).

name: Discovery of nuclear fission
summary: Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann discovered that uranium nuclei could split, releasing enormous energy and opening the nuclear age.
body:
The experiments were done in Berlin, but the theoretical explanation came from Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch, who calculated that a splitting uranium nucleus would release some 200 million electron volts, millions of times the energy of any chemical reaction between the same atoms.

Splitting a heavy nucleus had been thought impossible, but the chemical evidence for barium among the products left no other explanation. Within months, physicists worldwide realised that a chain reaction was possible and that a bomb was conceivable. Einstein's letter to Roosevelt warning of Nazi atomic weapons followed, and the race for the [atomic bomb](event:trinity) began.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fission).

name: World War II
summary: The deadliest conflict in history: some 70–85 million dead, fought across every ocean and most continents.
body:
Germany's invasion of Poland began it in Europe; [Barbarossa](event:barbarossa) and [Pearl Harbor](event:pearl-harbor) in 1941 made it global. The tide turned at [Stalingrad](event:stalingrad) and [Midway](event:midway); [D-Day](event:d-day) opened the Western Front; the [Holocaust](event:holocaust) murdered six million Jews.

It ended with the [atomic bombing of Hiroshima](event:hiroshima) weeks after the [Trinity test](event:trinity), opening the nuclear age and the [Cold War](event:cold-war) that followed.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II).

image.caption: US troops landing at Omaha Beach, 1944

name: Battle of Britain
summary: The RAF held off the Luftwaffe in the first campaign fought entirely in the air, ending the threat of invasion.
body:
Part of [World War II](event:ww2). The RAF held off the Luftwaffe in the first campaign fought entirely in the air, ending the threat of invasion.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Britain).

name: Operation Barbarossa
summary: Germany invaded the Soviet Union along a 2,900 km front — the largest invasion in history.
body:
Part of [World War II](event:ww2). Germany invaded the Soviet Union along a 2,900 km front — the largest invasion in history.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Barbarossa).

name: Attack on Pearl Harbor
summary: A Japanese carrier strike on the US Pacific Fleet brought the United States into the war.
body:
Part of [World War II](event:ww2). A Japanese carrier strike on the US Pacific Fleet brought the United States into the war.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_on_Pearl_Harbor).

name: The Holocaust
summary: Nazi Germany murdered six million Jews, along with Roma, disabled people, Soviet prisoners and political opponents.
body:
Part of [World War II](event:ww2). Mass shootings by the Einsatzgruppen gave way to industrialised killing at extermination camps, of which Auschwitz-Birkenau was the largest. The word *genocide* was coined to describe it, and the Genocide Convention of 1948 followed.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Holocaust).

name: Quit India Movement
summary: Gandhi's final major campaign for Indian independence demanded that Britain leave India immediately, galvanising the nation and hastening the end of the Raj.
body:
Part of [British Raj](event:british-raj). The British jailed Gandhi and thousands of other Congress leaders, but the movement — "Do or Die" was Gandhi's slogan — could not be suppressed by imprisonment alone.

[World War II](event:ww2) had weakened Britain's grip, and the movement's moral force, rooted in non-violent resistance and decades of struggle, proved irresistible. Within five years of Quit India, the [British Raj](event:british-raj) ended and [India had won independence](event:indian-independence).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quit_India_Movement).

name: Battle of Stalingrad
summary: The turning point of the Eastern Front; the German Sixth Army was encircled and destroyed in the ruined city.
body:
Part of [World War II](event:ww2). Roughly **two million** casualties made it one of the bloodiest battles in history. The Soviet counter-offensive *Operation Uranus* closed the ring in November 1942; Paulus surrendered in February.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Stalingrad).

name: Battle of Midway
summary: American carriers sank four Japanese fleet carriers in a single day, reversing the balance in the Pacific.
body:
Part of [World War II](event:ww2). American carriers sank four Japanese fleet carriers in a single day, reversing the balance in the Pacific.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Midway).

name: D-Day landings
summary: The largest amphibious operation ever mounted put 156,000 Allied troops ashore in Normandy in one day.
body:
Part of [World War II](event:ww2). The largest amphibious operation ever mounted put 156,000 Allied troops ashore in Normandy in one day.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normandy_landings).
